content: Recent advancements in technology, including the widespread availability of mobile phones and portable computers, as well as improvements in the accessibility features of these devices, have provided children and young people with low vision greater opportunities for independent access to information. Established electronic technologies, such as closed-circuit television (CCTV), have long been used as low vision aids. Newer devices, such as electronic readers and commercially available tablet computers, may offer similar functionalities while being more portable and cost-effective. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of electronic assistive technologies (ATs) on reading ability, educational outcomes, and quality of life in children and young people with low vision. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Health Technology Assessment Programme, the metaRegister of Controlled Trials, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. The search covered publications from January 1946 to October 2014, with no restrictions on language or publication date. The final search was completed on October 30, 2014. The inclusion criteria for this review specified randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs involving children aged 5 to 16 years with low vision, as defined by the World Health Organization's 1992 definition. The studies needed to investigate the use of assistive technologies, including various types of CCTV/electronic vision enhancement systems (EVES), computer technologies such as tablet computers, and adaptive technologies like screen readers, screen magnifiers, and optical character recognition (OCR) systems. Comparisons were planned between ATs and standard optical aids, such as refractive correction for distance vision, monocular/binocular devices for distance viewing, and brightfield magnifiers for near vision. Additionally, comparisons between different types of ATs, with or without conventional optical aids, and the impact of providing ATs with or without usage instructions were also intended. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies by screening titles and abstracts. Studies were categorized as 'definitely include,' 'definitely exclude,' or 'possibly include.' Full-text versions of studies in the 'possibly include' category were obtained for further evaluation, and final inclusion or exclusion decisions were made collaboratively by the reviewers. No randomized controlled trials were identified in this area of research. The authors concluded that there is a lack of high-quality evidence regarding the effectiveness of electronic assistive technologies for children and young people with visual impairment. This evidence is crucial to guide healthcare providers, educators, and families in making informed decisions about selecting appropriate technologies. Future research should include randomized controlled trials to evaluate the impact of assistive technologies. Research protocols should prioritize outcomes that are meaningful not only to the scientific community but also to families and educators. Functional outcomes, such as reading accuracy, comprehension, and speed, should be measured, along with the effects of assistive technologies on independent learning and overall quality of life.
